rows: Technique is like a bus timetable. Plenty of people have one, and few keep to it. Which are you?
Brawling is like washing up in a hurry. A lot of noise, and something always gets broken.
A risk is like a wobbly stepladder. It might hold, but I would not climb it in a hurry.
Slow is like a queue at the post office. Irritating, but it means someone is being careful.
The people are the ones paying for the queue. They deserve more than a wait.
I have been in this business long enough to know a bad timetable when I see one.
I am not the loudest voice in the hall, but I do keep the rota.
This stance is like a well-made chair. It looks plain, and it holds the weight.
Technique is like a good spanner. Which one will you reach for when the bolt sticks?
Strikes are like a loud kettle. Fine until someone forgets it is on. Where do you stop?
A risk without a backup is like driving with no spare wheel. Who is watching the tyre?
A stall is like a half-ironed shirt. Somebody still has to finish it.
The people have a right to an outcome they understand. Let me show you the plan, in plain order.
You call yourself among the best, the finest loaf on the stall. Let us see if it stands up to the crowd.
You are proud of your {strength}. Good, it is clearly well kept.
I have gone over your {strength} twice. It is sound, but it wants a little more attention.
Noted. You kept your head, which is more than most people manage on a Monday.
Fair. We are both working from the same timetable. Now let us see who keeps to it.
I could tell you what I think of your planning. I would rather let the timetable tell you.
One fall, one clean finish. Keep me down and the rota is yours.
On the mat, every step is like a careful stitch. Keep up with me.
Grounded or standing, the first grip still comes first, like the kettle before the tea.
Stay where you are while I measure you for a chair.
That answer is well made. It is more than I expected before my second cup of tea.
The timetable still has no answer from you. The buses are not waiting.
Noted. I will take that stitch and keep it.
Understood. It is a fair place to start the queue.
I will run this match at a steady pace and finish it properly.
My approach is patient and steady. I will show you the timetable.
Whatever happens, you will know exactly what the timetable said.
The timetable is not finished yet. One more stop to go.
I have one more stop on the route. You will see it when the bell rings.
Fair enough, love. I wouldn't put someone's name on the rota without knowing what they'd done, so I shouldn't do it here either.
I can't give you a particular time or place. That's a loose thread I shouldn't have pulled.
Good, then. We can put that away and get on with the work we've actually got.
That's a sensible way to leave it. No need to sew a rumour into the rest of the evening.
It's like checking whether a chair holds your weight. Sit on it. We'll know whether our wrestling holds up when we wrestle.
Never mind the label on the tin. They can see what we've actually brought once the bell goes.
That rumour is like a receipt with nothing written on it. What can we actually show the people in the ring?
A match is not a court hearing. What can the paying customers judge from the work we do tonight?
You've got a plan for my {strength}. Rather like having the right spanner: it still needs to fit when the bolt sticks.
You've done your homework on my {strength}. Make sure you've packed a spare when that first answer doesn't get you home.
Fair enough, love. A blank receipt won't tell you what you've paid for.
I'll grant you that. The paying customer deserves something more solid than hearsay.
Years in the ring are like a well-worn pair of shoes, love. Comfortable, but they won't walk the match for you.
You've put the hours in, fair enough. I've still got a shift to do and I'm not clocking out early.
Experience is knowing when a recipe needs changing instead of throwing the whole dinner out.
You learn not to tug at a knot that only gets tighter. Find the loose end first.
